newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian doctor warns of euthanasia panic.
newsitem.headline: Australian doctor warns of euthanasia panic.

text.p: Australian euthanasia campaigners announced the death of a fourth person under the world's only euthanasia law on Tuesday and said other terminally ill patients were panicking that the law might soon be overturned.

A 70-year-old Sydney woman committed suicide under the voluntary euthanasia law in the remote Northern Territory on the weekend, The National Coalition for Voluntary Euthanasia said on Tuesday on its Internet site "Deliverance".
The unidentified woman, who suffered from cancer, died in the Territory's capital Darwin using a machine which delivered a lethal injection, the coalition said.
The voluntary euthanasia law came into operation in the outback region in July last year. In September, 66-year-old cancer patient Bob Dent became the first person to use it.

But the Australian parliament's lower house, the House of Representatives, has since passed a bill aimed at overturning the euthanasia law and the upper house Senate is expected to vote on it this month.
Euthanasia is illegal in the rest of Australia, but doctors say it is widely practised.

"Terminally ill patients who are establishing their eligibility under the Territory law are becoming extremely anxious and beginning to panic," said Dr Philip Nitschke, who has assisted all four people to die using the euthanasia law.
"They realise that the possibility exists for the law to be cut from under them before they have a chance to benefit from it," Nitschke said on the Internet site.
Nitschke, dubbed "Doctor Death" by anti-euthanasia groups, told Reuters that a number of terminally-ill patients had already gained the three medical signatures necessary to use the euthanasia law.

"These patients have enough difficulty battling and dealing with the suffering from their terminal illness without having now to deal with the additional anxiety brought about by the senate vote," said Nitschke.

"Some patients have established their eligibility and they are now confronted with the impossible situation of having to decide whether to go ahead prematurely and use the act (law) before the vote is taken in the senate during March."
Nitschke said that he expected "several" people would be legally ready to use the euthanasia law by the time the senate votes on the anti-euthanasia bill, expected in late March.
Nitschke called on the senate to make a public statement assuring terminally-ill patients that they should not feel pressured to decide to use the euthanasia law.
"To offer these vulnerable people less than this is to behave in an inhuman, barbaric and essentially uncivilised manner, and will be a damning indictment of the Australian senate," he said.
Nitschke said Australia's federal politicans should be held responsible for any premature deaths.
Australian opinion polls show overwhelming public support for voluntary euthanasia, but a private member's bill aimed at overturning the controversial law has attracted bi-partisan political support.
Under Australia's constitution the national government can override laws in the country's three territories, but not its six states.
